hints: Start by drawing out the structure of 2-methylbutan-1-ol and notice what type of alcohol group it has.
The -CH2OH group tells you it is primary, so think about what primary alcohols do with PCl5 and with mild oxidation.
Now look closely at carbon 2 with its four different groups attached, and link that to the condition for chirality.
walkthrough:
**Draw the structure and classify the alcohol**

Great first move is always to sketch it. 2-methylbutan-1-ol is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

The OH is on a $\text{CH}_2$ group, so it is a primary alcohol. That one fact controls statement 2.

**Check statement 1, reaction with PCl5**

All alcohols, primary, secondary or tertiary, react with phosphorus pentachloride to replace OH by Cl.

$$\text{R-OH} + \text{PCl}_5 \rightarrow \text{R-Cl} + \text{POCl}_3 + \text{HCl(g)}$$ 
So steamy white fumes of $\text{HCl(g)}$ are seen. Statement 1 is correct.

**Check statement 2, oxidation to an aldehyde**

Primary alcohols oxidise first to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids.

$$\text{R-CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{[O]} \text{R-CHO} \xrightarrow{[O]} \text{R-COOH}$$ 
With controlled distillation we can stop at the aldehyde, 2-methylbutanal. Statement 2 is correct.

**Check statement 3, optical isomerism**

Look for a chiral carbon with four different groups. Focus on C-2:

$$\text{C-2 attached to: H, CH}_3, \text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3, \text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$
All four are different, so C-2 is a chiral centre. The molecule exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images. Statement 3 is correct.

**Combine the conclusions**

Since 1, 2 and 3 are all correct, the combination that includes all three statements is the answer.

options.A: Correct, because all three statements are true. It gives HCl with PCl5, it is primary so oxidises to 2-methylbutanal, and C-2 is chiral so it shows optical isomerism.
options.B: Incorrect, because it misses statement 3. Many students think branching prevents chirality, but C-2 has H, CH3, CH2CH3 and CH2OH, four different groups, so it is definitely chiral.
options.C: Incorrect, because it misses statement 1. Some students only associate PCl5 with testing for carboxylic acids, but all alcohols give HCl(g) with PCl5.
options.D: Incorrect, because it includes only statement 1. This comes from misclassifying the alcohol as secondary or tertiary and thinking it cannot form an aldehyde, and from overlooking the chiral centre at C-2.
